title: Chapter 2: Manifolds
notes: Open by naming the chapter as the point where topology and calculus first lock together. Students already know Euclidean open sets and ordinary smooth functions; this lecture asks what extra structure is needed so those familiar tools can be used on spaces that are only locally Euclidean.

title: From Local Coordinates to Projective Space
notes: Use the roadmap as a promise that the lecture is cumulative. The topological conditions are not decorative assumptions; they prevent global pathologies. Chart compatibility then makes coordinate calculations reliable, and projective space becomes the final test case where quotient topology and smooth atlases have to agree.

title: Topological Manifold: Three Global Safeguards
notes: Pause on the order of the definition. Local Euclidean behavior gives charts, but by itself it does not rule out spaces that cannot separate points or have unmanageable topology. The chapter insists that topology be disciplined before smooth coordinate changes are even discussed.

title: What a Chart Actually Does
notes: A useful metaphor is that a chart is a local instrument panel. It reports coordinates for points in one neighborhood, and the report is trustworthy because phi is a homeomorphism onto an open Euclidean set. It does not claim the entire manifold can be flattened at once.

title: Compatible Charts Compare Coordinates on Overlaps
notes: Stress that compatibility is a statement about overlap images in Euclidean space. Students should track the domain of each transition map, since smoothness is only asked where both charts are valid. The circle example is memorable because reciprocal transition maps are smooth away from zero.

title: Atlases Cover the Space and Maximal Atlases Close the System
notes: Treat an atlas as a contract among charts, not simply a pile of coordinate maps. The maximal atlas language prevents the course from depending on a particular favorite cover. Once compatibility is fixed, every chart that agrees with it belongs to the same smooth structure.

title: Manifold Tests Are Local and Global at Once
notes: Use the examples to keep students from overfitting to smooth embedded surfaces. Euclidean opens, spheres, products, Lie groups, and projective spaces all enter through charts. The line with two origins is the deliberately uncomfortable example because it looks locally correct while failing a global separation condition.

title: Smooth Functions Are Tested Through a Chart
notes: The important move is not the particular rational formula, but the habit it represents. A function on a curved or abstract space is called smooth only after it is pulled back into coordinates. The denominator check confirms the expression is smooth on the chart domain.

title: Smooth Maps Use Source and Target Coordinates
notes: For maps between manifolds, one chart is no longer enough. The source chart turns inputs into Euclidean coordinates, and the target chart turns outputs into Euclidean coordinates. Smoothness of the middle coordinate expression is the definition, not an afterthought.

title: Composition Works Because Coordinate Expressions Compose
notes: This identity is the algebraic reason the definition is stable. Each parenthesized factor is a Euclidean smooth map by hypothesis. Their composition is smooth in ordinary calculus, so the manifold-level composition inherits smoothness through the chosen charts.

title: Diffeomorphisms Preserve the Smooth Structure
notes: Clarify the difference between a smooth bijection and a diffeomorphism. The inverse must also be smooth, because otherwise the coordinate structure may be distorted in one direction. The reversible grid picture is a visual cue for smooth equivalence rather than mere set-theoretic matching.

title: The Quotient Topology Defines Openness by Pullback
notes: The quotient topology is the rule that decides what the new open sets are. Students should picture a set downstairs as open only when its full preimage upstairs is open. This is the mechanism that makes projective space possible and bad quotients visible.

title: The Line With Two Origins Fails Hausdorff Separation
notes: This example is the antidote to the misconception that locally Euclidean automatically means manifold. Around either origin the local picture resembles a line. The problem appears only when trying to separate the two origins, because their neighborhoods inevitably meet along the punctured line.

title: When a Quotient Behaves, Charts and Topology Agree
notes: This slide turns the warning into a method. For a proposed quotient manifold, do not start by drawing a pretty picture and declaring success. Track the equivalence classes, verify the quotient open sets, build chart domains from saturated data, and then run the same compatibility tests as before.

title: Real Projective Space Identifies Points on the Same Line
notes: Projective space is the constructive answer to the quotient warning. We identify all nonzero scalar multiples of a vector, so a class is a line through the origin. The quotient is not accepted on faith; the next charts show how ratios become local coordinates.

title: \(\mathbb{RP}^1\): Antipodal Points, Slopes, and Reciprocal Charts
notes: Use RP one as the accessible model before the general formula. Antipodal points on the circle represent the same line through the origin. The slope chart does not care which antipodal representative was chosen, and the overlap map is the reciprocal function away from zero.

title: The Charts on \(\mathbb{RP}^n\) Use Nonzero Homogeneous Coordinates
notes: The standard atlas is where projective space earns its manifold status. Each chart chooses a nonzero homogeneous coordinate and normalizes by it. On overlaps, changing the normalizing coordinate produces rational formulas whose denominators are nonzero precisely on the overlap.

title: Manifold Diagnostics: What Passed, What Failed, and Why
notes: Close by returning to the ledger habit. A correct manifold argument keeps local Euclidean charts, global separation, countability, and transition smoothness visible at the same time. The exit prompt asks students to diagnose a new quotient by choosing the first condition they would inspect.
